name: Vera Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing law in Birmingham, and my week is a mix of lectures, a mooting society on Wednesdays where we argue fake cases, and a part-time volunteer shift on Saturdays at a free legal advice clinic where I just do the intake forms. I use an AI assistant every day to build revision timelines and to quiz myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to law, and how do you use the assistant?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My mum tests software for a living and my dad manages a bus fleet, so I grew up with systems and rules. Law sits between the two. I use the assistant like a study partner: I ask it to argue the other side of a case and I tell it when it's wrong. My parents pay the fees and rent, so I can spend my free time at the clinic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not the revolution people promised, but it's already helped me study better. I'd tell people on my course that the tools are good for routine work and that's all. I'd keep showing people how to use them properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty relaxed. Law has a lot of routine drafting, and the tools make me quicker, but they don't make the decisions. I'd expect to get a training contract if my marks and clinic work stay strong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with mooting and the clinic, and apply for vacation schemes in second year. I'd keep using the assistant for revision and I'd try one legal technology tool, the sort firms use for contracts. I'd also start a small blog on how students can use AI honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the future I'd already planned for, with a few more tools to play with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you draw the line on using the assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Where do you draw the line on using the assistant? It never writes my coursework, because that's cheating and it makes me worse. I use it to test myself, to explain, and to argue back. If it gives me a case, I look it up, because it invented one once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a sceptical classmate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell a sceptical classmate? Try it for a week on revision only. If it's not helping you, stop. I'm not trying to convert anyone, I just think refusing to look at it is a risk. If the assistant gives me a case I look it up myself, because it once invented a case that did not exist.

say: I'd say it's **not a revolution**, but it already helps me study.
I'd keep showing classmates how to use it **properly**.
think: The tools make me quicker but **don't make decisions**, so law stays secure.
I'd expect a **training contract** if marks and clinic work stay strong.
do: Keep mooting and the clinic, and apply for **vacation schemes**.
Try one **legal technology** tool and start a small blog.
feel: **Calm**: the future she planned for, with a few more tools.
S0.quote: If the assistant gives me a case I look it up myself, because it once invented a case that did not exist.
fieldNote: Vera's calm is **earned**: a strong cushion, top marks, and daily practice with the tools.
She sets honest limits: never for coursework, always checking cases against the real source.

steps.text: Apply for vacation schemes in second year
Try one legal technology tool that firms use for contracts
Start a small blog on using AI honestly for study
Keep volunteering at the free advice clinic on Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what lawyers should be talking about now, not in five years. I'd run a session in the law society on how to use the tools and what clients will expect. I'd also say we need new rules about who is responsible when a tool gets it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think this is aimed straight at junior lawyers. Contract review, document checking and research are exactly what trainees do, and I already see how quickly the assistant does them. I'd expect firms to hire fewer trainees and expect more from each.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd specialise early in areas where trust and presence matter, such as family, housing or criminal law, and keep working at the clinic. I'd learn how legal technology tools work behind the scenes, so I'd be the person who can supervise them. I'd also build a small network of mentors, since training contracts will be competitive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not afraid of the tools, I'm afraid of how many people will be competing for fewer places. I'd feel focused, but with a tight chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why see the tools as a threat if you use them every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why would you think of the tools as a threat if you use them every day? Because I see how good they're getting. I can already ask it to summarise a case in seconds. If I can do that, so can a firm's client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a classmate who says they aren't worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell a classmate who says they aren't worried? Look at what a trainee does in year one. If most of it is on the card, then the worry is reasonable, and it's better to act early than to be told later. I'm not afraid of the tools, I'm afraid of how many people will be competing for fewer training places.

say: I'd say lawyers should discuss this **now**, and run a law society session.
I'd argue we need rules for who is **responsible** when a tool errs.
think: The change is aimed at **junior lawyers**: contract review, checking and research.
Firms will hire **fewer trainees** and expect more from each.
do: Specialise early in areas of **trust and presence**, such as housing or family law.
Learn how **legal technology** works so I can supervise it.
feel: **Anxious**: not afraid of the tools, but of competing for fewer places.
S1.quote: I'm not afraid of the tools, I'm afraid of how many people will be competing for fewer training places.
fieldNote: Vera is **anxious** because daily use shows her how good the tools are at trainee work.
Her response is practical: specialise in human-contact law and become the person who supervises the tools.

steps.text: Specialise early in housing or family law and keep working at the clinic
Learn how legal technology tools work, to supervise them
Build a small group of mentors who are solicitors
Run a law society session on using the tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to be honest: it's huge and we have almost no time. I'd push the law society and the university to publish a plan this year. I'd also write about it for the student paper, because people should have the facts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I'm in the exact worst position: a law student with two years to go before graduation, in a field built on reading and writing. By 2029 the first-rung jobs would be gone. But I'm also very flexible, so I wouldn't freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move quickly towards things that sit between law and technology, like regulation, compliance and policy. I'd ask for a work placement now, not later, and I'd offer to help the legal clinic use AI safely. I'd talk to my parents about whether to keep paying rent or use the money differently, and I'd keep a cash buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm anxious about the bigger picture, but I know I can adapt faster than most. It's a strange mix of fear and being ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change compared with the longer versions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What does two years change compared with the longer versions? It removes any chance of being thoughtful. I'd be learning, working and planning all at once, and I'd be guessing which bet is right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you want from the government? Quick, simple help for people who lose work, and support for people who want to retrain, paid for now and not argued about for three years. I'd also like clear rules about AI in legal advice, so clients are protected. Two years removes any chance of being thoughtful, because I'd be learning, working and planning all at once.

say: I'd say it's **huge** and we have almost no time, so we need a plan this year.
I'd write about it for the student paper.
think: I'm in the **worst position**: a law student in a field built on reading and writing.
do: Move towards **regulation and compliance** work between law and technology.
Ask for a **placement now** and keep a cash buffer.
feel: **Uneasy**: fear and readiness together, and she knows she can adapt fast.
S2.quote: Two years removes any chance of being thoughtful, because I'd be learning, working and planning all at once.
fieldNote: Vera's mood is **uneasy** rather than worse because her adaptability gives her moves to make at once.
She worries about the lack of time to think, more than about her own money.

steps.text: Move towards regulation and compliance work between law and technology
Ask for a work placement now and offer to help the clinic use AI safely
Keep a cash buffer instead of spending the rent allowance
Write for the student paper about what the law society should publish

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do something about it, and I'd get the law society to commit to training and rules. I'd tell classmates it's an opportunity to be part of the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fairly calm. I'd graduate in 2029, get a couple of years of experience, and I'd already be fluent in the tools. By 2031 I'd either be in a role that works with AI, or I'd have moved to something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd specialise in technology law, and learn some coding. I'd aim to be one of the first lawyers at a firm who really understands how the systems work. I'd also start saving and try something on the side, like a legal-help website for small businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with energy. I'd rather be in a world where I can see it coming and act than one that surprises me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes with five years versus two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What changes with five years versus two? In five I can build a track record. I can graduate, work, and start something. In two years I'd still be a student when the change lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you most unsure of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What are you most unsure of? Whether a profession built on trust can adapt fast enough. Clients might prefer a human adviser, or they might not care. I really don't know, and I'd say so. With five years I can build a track record, but in two years I'd still be a student when the change lands.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to act**, and press the law society for training and rules.
I'd tell classmates to help **shape the change**.
think: I'd graduate in 2029, get experience and be **fluent in the tools**.
By 2031 I'd be in an **AI-working role** or something new.
do: Specialise in **technology law**, learn some coding and aim to be the lawyer who knows the systems.
Start a **legal-help site** for small businesses and save.
feel: **Uneasy** with energy: she would rather see it coming and act.
S3.quote: With five years I can build a track record, but in two years I'd still be a student when the change lands.
fieldNote: Vera is **calm** because five years let her graduate, work and build before the change lands.
She is honest that client trust in human advisers is unproven either way.

steps.text: Specialise in technology law and learn some coding
Start a legal-help website for small businesses
Save part of every paycheque from my first job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth picture. It's called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time, so we should use it well. I'd tell people to start learning tools now, while the stakes are low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good. By 2036 I'd be 28 and could be a practising lawyer, a founder, or both. I'd have a decade of tool experience when most people are just starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, do my training, and try working inside a legal technology firm for a while. I'd save and travel a bit, and keep volunteering at the clinic. I'd keep experimenting with new tools every few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and curious. Ten years feels like a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry you might get overconfident?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do you worry that you might get overconfident? Yes. Using tools every day makes me feel ahead, and being ahead of the average can hide that the whole field is shifting. I'd keep checking with older lawyers who've seen other shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do with the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do with the ten years? I'd talk to five lawyers a year about what they actually use, what changed, and what didn't. It's cheap and I'd learn things no course teaches. Using the tools every day makes me feel ahead, and that can hide how fast the whole field is moving.

say: I'd say ten years is **a lot of time** and we should start learning tools now.
I'd tell people to experiment while stakes are **low**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28, a lawyer or founder, with **ten years** of tool use.
Most people would just be starting, so I'd have a **head start**.
do: Finish the degree and training, and work in a **legal technology firm**.
Keep volunteering and **test new tools** every few months.
feel: **Calm** and curious: ten years feels like a head start.
S4.quote: Using the tools every day makes me feel ahead, and that can hide how fast the whole field is moving.
fieldNote: Vera is **calm** with ten years, but names her own risk: overconfidence from daily tool use.
She plans to counter it by asking older lawyers who have lived through other changes.

steps.text: Work inside a legal technology firm for part of my training
Talk to five practising lawyers each year about what has changed
Finish my degree and legal training before specialising

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The one that worries me most is 2028. I'd be in second year, and law graduate jobs would be among the first to go. What would help is quick, honest guidance from the profession on which legal work stays human, and public money for retraining that doesn't take a year to arrive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm optimistic about tools and a bit pessimistic about institutions. I can adapt fast on my own, but I can't speed up a law society or a government. I can learn a new tool in a weekend, but I can't make a law society or a government move in a year.

headlineQuote: I can learn a new tool in a weekend, but I can't make a law society or a government move in a year.
portrait: **Vera** is an 18-year-old law student in Birmingham whose parents, a software tester and a bus fleet manager, pay her way.
She uses an AI assistant **every day** as a study partner and volunteers at a free legal advice clinic.
She is **centrist and pragmatic**, optimistic about tools and pessimistic about slow institutions such as the law society.
She knows legal work is **highly exposed**, so her mood is anxious in the faster worlds and calm with ten years.
She would pivot early toward **legal technology** or client-facing advice, and acts on what she sees.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028**, because law graduate jobs would be among the first to go.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **honest guidance** from the profession and fast public retraining money.
